title: The Antarctic had a quiet summer, and got an explanation saying it should not last

blocks.text: This round covers the cryosphere and the ocean over the weeks around mid-May 2026. The window is honestly thin for headline announcements: the big sea-ice numbers were released in March, and the annual ocean-heat and glacier assessments came out in January and February. So the window was widened to mid-April through mid-May, which catches one substantial new paper (8 May), the European State of the Climate (28 April) and the World Glacier Monitoring Service's 2025 figures (15 April). The join is what this round adds: those releases put next to what our own copies of the underlying series actually say.
THE ANTARCTIC HAD A QUIET SUMMER

NSIDC reported that Antarctic sea ice reached its 2026 minimum of 2.58 million km2 on 26 February 2026, the sixteenth lowest in the 48-year satellite record. That is 260,000 km2 below the 1981-2010 average but 730,000 km2 above the record low set on 21 February 2023. Ted Scambos of CIRES attributed the near-average outcome to strong southerly winds in January and February pushing ice outward in the Weddell Sea. Published 2026-03-09.

Our own copy of the NSIDC Sea Ice Index monthly file (S_02, version 4, re-read from the NSIDC server on 2026-08-09) gives a February 2026 monthly mean Antarctic extent of 2.91 million km2. The four preceding Februaries were 2.21 (2022), 1.98 (2023), 2.19 (2024) and 2.22 (2025). February 2026 is the highest monthly February mean since 2021.

Our reading: 2.58 and 2.91 are both NSIDC's, both correct, and they are not the same quantity. 2.58 is the lowest single daily value of the year (a five-day trailing average, dated 26 February). 2.91 is the mean over all 28 days of February. A round that quotes one number and charts the other has quietly changed the subject. We hold the monthly means because they are the series with a clean 48-year definition, and we cite the daily extremes as the daily extremes.

blocks.caption: ANTARCTIC SEA ICE, FEBRUARY MONTHLY MEAN, NSIDC SEA ICE INDEX V4 - THE 2026 VALUE IS 2.91 MILLION KM2

blocks.text: AND AN EXPLANATION THAT SAYS IT SHOULD NOT LAST

Narayanan et al., 'Compound drivers of Antarctic sea ice loss and Southern Ocean destratification', Science Advances volume 12 issue 19, published 8 May 2026, doi:10.1126/sciadv.aeb0166. Using an observationally constrained sea ice-ocean model over 2013-2023, the authors identify three phases: intensifying westerlies preconditioned the Southern Ocean through increased upwelling of warm, saline circumpolar deep water; strong winds in 2015-2016 mixed that water into the upper ocean and initiated the loss, particularly in East Antarctica; and sustained mixing plus reduced equatorward export of sea-ice-derived freshwater then held the system in an unprecedentedly low state. East Antarctic loss was primarily subsurface driven; West Antarctic loss was also forced by longwave radiative flux anomalies. The paper concludes that persistent upwelling-favourable conditions under anthropogenic forcing may push the Southern Ocean into a prolonged low sea ice state.

This converges with a study published seven weeks earlier: Spira et al., 'Wind-triggered Antarctic sea-ice decline preconditioned by thinning Winter Water', Nature Climate Change volume 16, published 18 March 2026. From roughly 110,000 hydrographic profiles, that paper finds the regime shift was preconditioned by a thinning of Antarctic Winter Water between 2005 and 2015, bringing warmer deep water closer to the surface, before anomalously strong winds in 2015 mixed across the thinned layer and broke down stratification.

Our reading: these two arrive at the same shape by different routes - one from a model constrained by observations, one from the hydrographic profiles themselves - and both say the trigger was wind acting on an ocean that had already been prepared for it over a decade. That matters for how you read a good year. If the mechanism is a shifted subsurface state, a single near-average summer produced by a favourable wind season is variability sitting on top of the shift, not the shift reversing. The two findings in this round are not in conflict; they are a mean and a wobble, and the papers are about the mean.

The boring reading, and it has two parts. First, Walt Meier of the NASA NSIDC DAAC said plainly on 9 March that this year's return to less extreme conditions is not unexpected given how large Antarctic year-to-year variation is, and one year is one year in either direction. Second, and less comfortable: the instrument changed. NSIDC Sea Ice Index Version 4, announced 31 July 2025, replaced SSMIS input with JAXA's AMSR2 (product NSIDC-0803) from 1 January 2025 onward, because access to DMSP SSMIS data was ending and the ageing sensors were degrading. NSIDC notes that AMSR2 typically places the ice edge slightly inboard of SSMIS, giving somewhat smaller extents. The source_dataset column in our own downloaded CSV shows the switch: NSIDC-0051 through 2024, NSIDC-0803 for 2025 and 2026. So the last two years of every sea-ice number in this round come from a different sensor than the previous forty-six, and the direction of that bias makes recent lows look slightly lower, not higher. It does not manufacture a rebound, but anyone reading a two-year change off this record should know it is there.
THE ARCTIC WENT THE OTHER WAY

NSIDC reported that Arctic sea ice reached its 2026 winter maximum of 14.29 million km2 on 15 March 2026, about 1.36 million km2 below the 1981-2010 average. That edges just below the 2025 maximum of 14.31 million km2 and is treated as a statistical tie, since NSIDC considers values within 40,000 km2 equivalent: two record-low winter maxima back to back in a 48-year record. Published 2026-03-26, jointly reported by NASA.

Our copy of the NSIDC monthly file (N_03, version 4) gives March monthly mean Arctic extent of 14.12 million km2 in 2025 and 14.13 million km2 in 2026 - effectively identical, and the two lowest March means in the record.

Our reading: the daily-maximum and monthly-mean views of the Arctic agree here, and that agreement is worth stating. In the Antarctic the two views told noticeably different stories this year (a sixteenth-lowest daily minimum alongside the highest February mean since 2021), because a short wind-driven episode can move a single day's extreme much further than it moves a month. When the daily extreme and the monthly mean point the same way, as in the Arctic, the finding is more robust than either number alone.

blocks.caption: ARCTIC SEA ICE, MARCH MONTHLY MEAN - 2025 AND 2026 ARE THE TWO LOWEST IN THE RECORD

blocks.text: THE OCEAN KEPT TAKING THE HEAT

Pan, Cheng, Abraham, Trenberth, Reagan and colleagues, 'Ocean Heat Content Sets Another Record in 2025', Advances in Atmospheric Sciences, published 9 January 2026, doi:10.1007/s00376-026-5876-0. Global upper 2000 m ocean heat content increased by about 23 plus or minus 8 zettajoules relative to 2024 on the IAP/CAS estimate. About 16 percent of the global ocean area reached a record-high heat content, and about 33 percent ranked in its top three warmest since 1958. The paper reports 0-2000 m warming rising from 0.14 plus or minus 0.03 W m-2 per decade over 1960-2025 to 0.32 plus or minus 0.14 W m-2 per decade over 2005-2025.

Our own series is the independent NOAA NCEI world-ocean 0-2000 m yearly file, not IAP's. It gives 30.316 x 10^22 J for 2024 and 32.533 x 10^22 J for 2025 against the 1955-2006 average - an increase of 22.2 zettajoules.

Our reading: 22.2 ZJ from NOAA NCEI against 23 plus or minus 8 ZJ from IAP/CAS is close agreement between two independently constructed products, which use different gap-filling and different mapping choices over the same sparse Argo float array. Neither is a check on the other in a strict sense, since they share most of the same underlying profiles, but the year-on-year change agreeing to within a zettajoule means the 2025 jump is a property of the observations rather than of one group's method. This is the number we would defend hardest in this round.

blocks.caption: OCEAN HEAT CONTENT 0-2000 M, NOAA NCEI, WITH THE PUBLISHED STANDARD ERROR AS THE BAND

blocks.text: LAND ICE, WHICH IS WHERE THE SEA LEVEL COMES FROM

The World Glacier Monitoring Service reports that glaciers outside the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets lost 408 plus or minus 132 Gt during hydrological year 2025, equivalent to 1.1 plus or minus 0.4 mm of sea-level rise. Annual loss averaged under 100 Gt over 1976-1995, about 230 Gt/yr over 1996-2015, and 390 Gt/yr over 2016-2025. Cumulative loss since 1975 stands at 9,583 plus or minus 1,211 Gt, or 26.4 plus or minus 3.3 mm of sea level. Largest absolute contributions came from High Mountain Asia, Alaska and the Russian Arctic. WGMS page updated 2026-04-15; the figures were published in the Climate Chronicles of Nature Reviews Earth and Environment and in the European State of the Climate 2025.

The European State of the Climate 2025, from the Copernicus Climate Change Service and the WMO, published 28 April 2026: the Greenland Ice Sheet lost 139 Gt of ice in 2025; every European glacier region showed net mass loss, with Iceland recording its second-largest loss on record; 86 percent of the European ocean region was affected by a marine heatwave and 36 percent experienced severe or extreme conditions, the highest proportion on record; and European sea surface temperature was the highest ever recorded, a fourth consecutive year of record warmth.

The boring reading on the glacier number: 408 Gt carries an uncertainty of plus or minus 132 Gt, which is about a third of the value, and that is not decoration. The global annual figure is not a measurement of the world's glaciers; it is a geostatistical model that combines in-situ mass-balance anomalies from a few hundred monitored glaciers with long-term remote-sensing trends over the other two hundred thousand. The long-term acceleration - under 100, then 230, then 390 Gt/yr across three periods - is far larger than the error bar and survives easily. A single year's value against the year before it does not, and should not be read as a trend.
WHAT WE COULD NOT CLOSE

Three things stayed open. There was no IMBIE reconciliation release or new GRACE-FO assessment in this window, so the ice-sheet mass numbers here remain NASA's standing 2002-2025 figures (about 264 Gt/yr for Greenland, about 135 Gt/yr for Antarctica) rather than anything new. Our satellite sea level series stops at early 2025 and so was not charted; NASA's own analysis of 2025, published 29 January 2026, found sea level rose only 0.08 cm during the year against a long-term expectation of 0.44 cm, which it attributed to La Nina moving water from ocean to land, and that is a fact about a single ENSO year rather than about the trend. And the WMO Global Annual to Decadal Climate Update covering 2026-2035 was published on 28 May 2026, after the date of this round, so it belongs to a later one.

knowledge: Established that the Antarctic 2026 daily minimum (2.58 million km2, NSIDC, 26 February) and the February monthly mean in our own series (2.91 million km2) are two different NSIDC quantities that must never be swapped, and recorded both. Cross-checked the 2025 ocean heat jump across two independent products: NOAA NCEI gives 22.2 ZJ, IAP/CAS gives 23 plus or minus 8 ZJ. Registered the Sea Ice Index v4 sensor change (SSMIS to AMSR2 from 2025-01-01) as a standing caveat on every recent sea-ice number we hold, verified in the source_dataset column of our own downloaded CSV. Added the WGMS 2025 glacier figure and the Narayanan et al. three-phase account of the Antarctic regime shift to the graph.
